title: FOREIGN KEY
description: Declare complete supported parent references with explicit actions and names, distinguish optional matching from presence, and verify native InnoDB constraints in disposable isolated databases.
notes:
## Declaration turns a modeled reference into an enforced rule

A foreign key declares that a child reference must match an accepted parent key under the engine's applicable rules. A campus employee can reference a department through department_id. A diagram may express that intended association, but the DDL must identify the actual child columns, parent table and referenced columns. Merely using the same column name does not create enforcement.

This topic focuses on declaration mechanics rather than treating every relationship line as automatic database behaviour. State which table owns the reference and what a valid parent identity means. If the model requires each employee to have a department, the child property also needs an appropriate required-value rule. Referential matching and mandatory presence are different constraints.

## The child column list maps to the parent list

A table-level FOREIGN KEY clause lists child roles and the corresponding referenced parent roles in order. For a department key composed of campus_id and department_id, both roles belong in the complete reference. A child with department_id 10 on Campus 2 must not accidentally match Department 10 on Campus 1 just because the local number is the same.

List arity and correspondence matter. Two child roles need two correctly ordered referenced roles, with supported compatible definitions. A composite declaration is not equivalent to two independent single-column references to unrelated candidate values. The full parent identity must exist together, which is exactly what the identifying pair expresses in the campus model.

```sql
CONSTRAINT fk_employee_department
  FOREIGN KEY (campus_id, department_id)
  REFERENCES departments (campus_id, department_id)
  ON DELETE RESTRICT
```

## Parent identity needs a supported target key

The examples reference a parent primary key, which provides a clear unique required identity. Appropriate unique keys can also serve supported references under the engine's rules. MySQL has historical and version-specific behaviour around nonstandard referenced keys, so it is inaccurate to present every legacy extension as a portable design recommendation.

Choose a supported unique parent identity deliberately and verify the target version's requirements. Matching index availability, column ordering and storage-engine support all matter. A parent column containing unique values in today's sample is not the same as a declared supported key that protects future state. The reference should rely on the actual enforced definition rather than a coincidental three-row observation.

## Type and comparison compatibility must be checked

Child and parent roles need compatible definitions under the target engine. Integer size and signedness can matter, and character references can depend on supported character-set and collation compatibility. A diagram showing both roles as a generic identifier does not prove the physical declarations meet those rules. Inspect the actual columns rather than infer compatibility from similar labels.

The exercises use matching integer definitions to keep that contract visible. A more complex schema using text codes needs its own exact definitions and native checks. Do not silently cast away a modeling mismatch in a query and claim the foreign key is established. A SELECT join can match transformed values without creating or validating a persistent reference constraint.

## NULL matching does not establish mandatory participation

For an ordinary optional single-column reference in the illustrated MySQL form, NULL does not require a matching parent value. That allows an employee whose department has not been assigned under an optional relationship policy. It does not claim that a parent row with a NULL primary key exists, and it does not turn the relationship into mandatory participation.

Composite NULL rules depend on the supported match semantics. MySQL's ordinary behaviour should not be generalized into every product's MATCH FULL or other modes. The composite exercise instead makes both roles required so incomplete parent identities cannot enter the accepted child table. State the chosen policy rather than relying on ambiguous partly missing pairs.

## Referential actions describe parent changes

ON DELETE CASCADE removes matching child rows when the referenced parent deletion is accepted under that rule. RESTRICT or relevant NO ACTION behaviour can block a parent change under the product's enforcement timing. SET NULL requires child columns and the model to permit the resulting missing reference. Each action encodes a domain policy, not a generic performance preference.

ON UPDATE actions concern changes to referenced key values under supported semantics. They are different from updating an unrelated parent description such as department_name. The exact set of supported actions and timing differs by engine. Do not assume SET DEFAULT or deferred checking works merely because the phrase appears in another product's documentation.

## Adding a reference must address existing child state

A populated child table can contain proposals whose parent identity is absent. Adding an enforced foreign key with normal validation requires a compatible current state under the target's rules. Resolve orphaned facts through an accepted domain workflow rather than deleting them arbitrarily or disabling checks to force the alteration to pass.

A diagnostic anti-existence query can help identify missing parents, but it is not itself a foreign key. It observes supplied rows at one point and does not protect later writes. Under concurrent traffic, preparation and enforcement need a consistent transition policy. The lab fixtures are isolated and single-session, so they do not claim to establish every production validation or locking guarantee.

## Naming supports deliberate maintenance

A descriptive constraint name makes the protected association easier to identify in catalog output and maintenance scripts. In MySQL, dropping a named reference uses ALTER TABLE child DROP FOREIGN KEY constraint_name. Removing the foreign-key constraint and removing a supporting index are different operations; inspect what remains rather than assuming one keyword always removes every related structure.

Dropping the reference changes accepted future writes even if no current row changes. Applications may rely on rejected orphan proposals or automatic actions, so maintenance is part of the shared data contract. A migration review should identify those consumers before treating a foreign-key removal as a harmless way to make a failing import succeed.

## Storage engine and object kind affect enforcement

MySQL/InnoDB supports the relevant persistent reference behaviour. Other storage engines and older inline-reference syntax can differ, including cases where written syntax does not establish the intended rule. Accepted CREATE text alone is therefore weaker evidence than a real invalid child write being rejected. Verify the actual definition and behaviour on the engine being claimed.

Temporary tables also have restrictions that make them unsuitable proof of native persistent foreign keys in this tutorial. These exercises therefore create fixed disposable databases with persistent InnoDB parent and child tables on the isolated lab server. Their temporary input tables only supply synthetic fixture values. This keeps native enforcement separate from a query mirror or an ignored temporary declaration.

## The simple exercise isolates optional references

The introductory task copies supplied departments and employees into known disposable parent and child tables. A required employee identity is separate from a nullable department reference. Valid employees match accepted departments, while an employee with NULL department remains permitted by the stated optional policy. A later nonmissing unknown department is rejected through the actual reference.

Each fixture resets only its own named disposable child and parent rows in dependency order before loading new inputs. This is an authorized laboratory arrangement, not an instruction to clear application tables. The prepared content migration stores the task and reference code as teaching content; it does not execute that laboratory reset against the application's shared database.

## The composite exercise verifies scoped cascading

The medium task uses departments keyed by campus_id and department_id and children carrying the same complete pair. It deletes one specified parent pair and reads the surviving employees. Departments with the same local number on another campus are separate parents, so their employees must remain. This exposes incorrect single-role matching and overly broad cleanup.

Negative cases attempt a child whose complete parent pair is absent. An existing department_id elsewhere is not enough. Empty input and a fixture without the selected parent exercise harmless absence under the requested delete predicate. Recorded results establish the supported native InnoDB behaviour on the compatibility engine, not exact MySQL execution or every possible referential action.

## Keep native evidence attached to its actual target

A useful structural illustration labels owner keys, child references and the exact action being tested. The notes, declarations and expected outputs should preserve the same campus scope. Otherwise a technically valid SQL clause can enforce a different relationship from the one students were taught to model.

The recorded MariaDB lab checks include real persistent InnoDB references and selected rejected writes, clearly labeled as compatibility-engine evidence. Exact MySQL/provider execution, other native engines, production concurrency and application migration application remain unverified. Earlier recorded native-action checks remain separate historical evidence; these new exercise cases do not silently expand them into a claim that every referential action or deployment scenario has passed.

questions.question_text: Which SQL clause form is required when a foreign key references a composite (multi-column) primary key in the parent table?
options: Column-level REFERENCES on each child column separately
The table-level FOREIGN KEY (col1, col2) REFERENCES parent(col1, col2) clause
Two separate single-column foreign keys
A CHECK constraint combined with REFERENCES
questions.explanation: A composite foreign key must be declared as one table-level FOREIGN KEY clause listing all referencing and referenced columns together; it cannot be split across column-level REFERENCES clauses.

questions.question_text: What happens when you attempt to add a FOREIGN KEY constraint to a populated table that contains rows whose FK column value has no matching row in the parent table?
options: The orphaned rows are automatically deleted
The orphaned rows' FK column is automatically set to NULL
The ALTER TABLE statement fails until the orphan rows are resolved
The constraint is added but disabled for those rows
questions.explanation: Adding a FOREIGN KEY validates all existing rows against the parent table; any orphan reference causes the statement to fail.

questions.question_text: Under the illustrated ordinary optional single-column MySQL reference, does NULL require a parent match?
options: Yes, always
No; the optional NULL marker does not require a corresponding parent value
Only if the parent table is empty
Only in PostgreSQL
questions.explanation: Composite match modes and required participation need separate definitions.

questions.question_text: Which ON DELETE action causes child rows to be automatically deleted when the referenced parent row is deleted?
options: RESTRICT
SET NULL
CASCADE
NO ACTION
questions.explanation: ON DELETE CASCADE propagates the delete operation to matching child rows; RESTRICT/NO ACTION block the delete instead.

questions.question_text: Which referenced-key choice is used for supported unambiguous identity in these examples?
options: They must be of type INT
They must be indexed with a non-unique index
The parent primary key or an appropriate supported unique key
They must be NOT NULL only, uniqueness is not required
questions.explanation: Historical MySQL nonstandard-key extensions should not be treated as a universal portable rule.

questions.question_text: In MySQL, which statement correctly drops a foreign key constraint named fk_orders_customer?
options: ALTER TABLE orders DROP CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer;
ALTER TABLE orders DROP FOREIGN KEY fk_orders_customer;
ALTER TABLE orders REMOVE FOREIGN KEY fk_orders_customer;
DROP FOREIGN KEY fk_orders_customer ON orders;
questions.explanation: MySQL requires the DROP FOREIGN KEY clause specifically, distinct from the DROP CONSTRAINT syntax used by PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server.

questions.question_text: Why verify actual enforcement rather than trust accepted foreign-key-looking text?
options: Because foreign keys were never part of the SQL standard
Storage engine, syntax form, object kind and version can determine whether the intended rule exists
Because the column names don't match exactly
Because MySQL requires foreign keys to be added only via ALTER TABLE, never CREATE TABLE
questions.explanation: A rejected orphan write provides stronger evidence than parser acceptance.

questions.question_text: What does this constraint-syntax topic emphasize?
options: This chapter explains why referential integrity matters conceptually
Child and parent role lists, naming, supported actions and validation against accepted state
This chapter only discusses foreign keys in the context of normalization
There is no difference; the two chapters cover identical material
questions.explanation: The declaration must implement the same modeled reference rather than merely draw a relationship line.

questions.question_text: Which roles identify Department 10 on Campus 2 in the composite model?
options: department_id=10 alone
Both campus_id=2 and department_id=10
The department label alone
Any campus number
questions.explanation: The local number is scoped by campus.

questions.question_text: Does a correct SELECT join create a foreign-key constraint?
options: Yes
Only with aliases
No
Only when ordered
questions.explanation: Query matching and accepted-state enforcement differ.

questions.question_text: What must SET NULL be compatible with?
options: Only output sorting
Only parent text length
The child nullability and optional relationship policy
Every mandatory key automatically
questions.explanation: The action cannot honestly preserve a required reference by making it absent.

questions.question_text: What does a rejected orphan insert demonstrate in this native lab?
options: Exact hosted-provider compatibility
Every referential action
Production migration success
Actual reference enforcement for that supplied case on the recorded engine
questions.explanation: Native object evidence remains engine and case scoped.

questions.question_text: Why use persistent InnoDB objects for these foreign-key fixtures?
options: Temporary-table support is not proof of persistent reference enforcement
Every temporary declaration enforces all references
To mutate application data
To disable checks
questions.explanation: Object kind is part of the verification contract.

questions.question_text: What should a child reference match in a composite key?
options: Any independently existing component values
The complete corresponding parent tuple in the stated order
The largest parent id
An arbitrary row
questions.explanation: Both roles must identify one accepted parent.

questions.question_text: Which MySQL form drops a named reference?
options: DROP PRIMARY KEY always
SELECT DISTINCT
DROP FOREIGN KEY constraint_name in ALTER TABLE
DROP COLUMN in every case
questions.explanation: Foreign-key and index removal are different maintenance decisions.

questions.question_text: Does ON DELETE CASCADE describe a parent description edit?
options: Yes
Only with VARCHAR
Only if labels match
No
questions.explanation: It concerns deletion of referenced parent identity.

questions.question_text: Why clear disposable child rows before parent rows when resetting this lab?
options: To respect the dependency while preparing a fresh synthetic case
To bypass enforcement
To clear every application table
To remove the constraint
questions.explanation: The reset preserves rather than disables the relationship rule.

questions.question_text: Can a department on Campus 2 satisfy a Campus 1 pair reference automatically?
options: Yes, if local department numbers match
No
Only if sorted
Only with INT
questions.explanation: The complete scoped key matters.

questions.question_text: What does name-only parser acceptance fail to establish?
options: That text was accepted
The spelling of the statement
That the intended constraint is enforced on the actual object
The name supplied
questions.explanation: Inspect the definition and test behaviour.

questions.question_text: What remains outside these new checks?
options: The recorded cascade result
The supplied orphan rejection
The actual isolated InnoDB fixture
Exact MySQL/provider execution and untested actions
questions.explanation: Compatibility-native evidence is not universal verification.

coding_problems.title: Declare and exercise a native optional InnoDB reference
coding_problems.task: In an authorized isolated lab only, create fixed database cx_dbms_lab_fk_easy and persistent InnoDB departments/ employees with the definitions in the reference contract: department_id parent primary key; employee_id child primary key; nullable employee department_id referencing the parent. Before each copy, clear only these disposable child rows then parent rows, without disabling checks. Copy supplied inputs and return employee_id,department_id. Positive fixtures contain only matching nonmissing references or NULL.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE department_input (department_id INT PRIMARY KEY); CREATE TABLE employee_input (employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,department_id INT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO department_input VALUES (10); INSERT INTO employee_input VALUES (1,10),(2,NULL);
constraints: Persistent InnoDB native constraint in fixed disposable cx_dbms_lab_fk_easy only.
Administrative lab capability required; no application tables are targets.
edge_cases: A nonmissing unknown parent is rejected.
hints: Declare the parent before its child.
Do not confuse a nullable reference with required participation.
coding_problems.solution_sql: CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS cx_dbms_lab_fk_easy; CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cx_dbms_lab_fk_easy.departments (department_id INT PRIMARY KEY) ENGINE=InnoDB; CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cx_dbms_lab_fk_easy.employees (employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,department_id INT NULL,CONSTRAINT fk_easy_department FOREIGN KEY(department_id) REFERENCES cx_dbms_lab_fk_easy.departments(department_id)) ENGINE=InnoDB; DELETE FROM cx_dbms_lab_fk_easy.employees; DELETE FROM cx_dbms_lab_fk_easy.departments; INSERT INTO cx_dbms_lab_fk_easy.departments SELECT department_id FROM department_input; INSERT INTO cx_dbms_lab_fk_easy.employees SELECT employee_id,department_id FROM employee_input; SELECT employee_id,department_id FROM cx_dbms_lab_fk_easy.employees ORDER BY employee_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The actual persistent InnoDB child references the declared parent identity; positive and negative cases exercise optional matching without a query-only simulation.

validation_cases.seed_sql: INSERT INTO department_input VALUES (20); INSERT INTO employee_input VALUES (7,20);

coding_problems.title: Cascade only the complete selected parent identity
coding_problems.task: In fixed disposable database cx_dbms_lab_fk_pair, define persistent InnoDB departments with PRIMARY KEY(campus_id,department_id) and employees with required matching roles plus employee_id primary key. Declare a composite FOREIGN KEY with ON DELETE CASCADE. Reset only these disposable child then parent rows, copy compatible inputs, delete parent (1,10), and return surviving employee_id,campus_id,department_id. Never disable checks or touch application tables.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE department_input (campus_id INT NOT NULL,department_id INT NOT NULL,PRIMARY KEY(campus_id,department_id)); CREATE TABLE employee_input (employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,campus_id INT NOT NULL,department_id INT NOT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO department_input VALUES (1,10),(2,10),(1,20); INSERT INTO employee_input VALUES (1,1,10),(2,2,10),(3,1,20);
constraints: Only the complete selected parent identity is deleted.
The native child action is enforced by InnoDB.
edge_cases: Same local number on another campus survives.
Absent selected parent makes the targeted delete a no-op.
hints: List both child and parent roles in the same order.
Let the declared action handle matching children.
coding_problems.solution_sql: CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS cx_dbms_lab_fk_pair; CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cx_dbms_lab_fk_pair.departments (campus_id INT NOT NULL,department_id INT NOT NULL,PRIMARY KEY(campus_id,department_id)) ENGINE=InnoDB; CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cx_dbms_lab_fk_pair.employees (employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,campus_id INT NOT NULL,department_id INT NOT NULL,CONSTRAINT fk_pair_department FOREIGN KEY(campus_id,department_id) REFERENCES cx_dbms_lab_fk_pair.departments(campus_id,department_id) ON DELETE CASCADE) ENGINE=InnoDB; DELETE FROM cx_dbms_lab_fk_pair.employees; DELETE FROM cx_dbms_lab_fk_pair.departments; INSERT INTO cx_dbms_lab_fk_pair.departments SELECT campus_id,department_id FROM department_input; INSERT INTO cx_dbms_lab_fk_pair.employees SELECT employee_id,campus_id,department_id FROM employee_input; DELETE FROM cx_dbms_lab_fk_pair.departments WHERE campus_id=1 AND department_id=10; SELECT employee_id,campus_id,department_id FROM cx_dbms_lab_fk_pair.employees ORDER BY employee_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The native composite reference ties children to the correct campus-scoped department, so the cascade preserves other parent identities.

validation_cases.seed_sql: INSERT INTO department_input VALUES (2,10); INSERT INTO employee_input VALUES (8,2,10);

original_questions.question_text: Which SQL clause form is required when a foreign key references a composite (multi-column) primary key in the parent table?
options: Column-level REFERENCES on each child column separately
The table-level FOREIGN KEY (col1, col2) REFERENCES parent(col1, col2) clause
Two separate single-column foreign keys
A CHECK constraint combined with REFERENCES
original_questions.explanation: A composite foreign key must be declared as one table-level FOREIGN KEY clause listing all referencing and referenced columns together; it cannot be split across column-level REFERENCES clauses.

original_questions.question_text: What happens when you attempt to add a FOREIGN KEY constraint to a populated table that contains rows whose FK column value has no matching row in the parent table?
options: The orphaned rows are automatically deleted
The orphaned rows' FK column is automatically set to NULL
The ALTER TABLE statement fails until the orphan rows are resolved
The constraint is added but disabled for those rows
original_questions.explanation: Adding a FOREIGN KEY validates all existing rows against the parent table; any orphan reference causes the statement to fail.

original_questions.question_text: By default, does a NULL value in a foreign key column violate the foreign key constraint?
options: Yes, always
No, NULL is exempt from FK matching regardless of parent table contents
Only if the parent table is empty
Only in PostgreSQL
original_questions.explanation: Foreign keys only validate non-NULL values against the parent; NULL is always permitted unless a separate NOT NULL constraint is also applied.

original_questions.question_text: Which ON DELETE action causes child rows to be automatically deleted when the referenced parent row is deleted?
options: RESTRICT
SET NULL
CASCADE
NO ACTION
original_questions.explanation: ON DELETE CASCADE propagates the delete operation to matching child rows; RESTRICT/NO ACTION block the delete instead.

original_questions.question_text: What must be true of the column(s) in the parent table that a FOREIGN KEY references?
options: They must be of type INT
They must be indexed with a non-unique index
They must be a PRIMARY KEY or carry a UNIQUE constraint
They must be NOT NULL only, uniqueness is not required
original_questions.explanation: A foreign key can only reference a column or column set that is guaranteed unique in the parent — either its PRIMARY KEY or a UNIQUE constraint.

original_questions.question_text: In MySQL, which statement correctly drops a foreign key constraint named fk_orders_customer?
options: ALTER TABLE orders DROP CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer;
ALTER TABLE orders DROP FOREIGN KEY fk_orders_customer;
ALTER TABLE orders REMOVE FOREIGN KEY fk_orders_customer;
DROP FOREIGN KEY fk_orders_customer ON orders;
original_questions.explanation: MySQL requires the DROP FOREIGN KEY clause specifically, distinct from the DROP CONSTRAINT syntax used by PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server.

original_questions.question_text: Why might a FOREIGN KEY clause in a CREATE TABLE statement be silently ignored in older MySQL setups?
options: Because foreign keys were never part of the SQL standard
Because the table uses a storage engine like MyISAM that does not support foreign key enforcement
Because the column names don't match exactly
Because MySQL requires foreign keys to be added only via ALTER TABLE, never CREATE TABLE
original_questions.explanation: Non-transactional storage engines like MyISAM parse but do not enforce FOREIGN KEY clauses; InnoDB is required for actual enforcement.

original_questions.question_text: What is the key syntactic difference this chapter's FOREIGN KEY discussion emphasizes compared to a prior chapter's coverage of foreign keys?
options: This chapter explains why referential integrity matters conceptually
This chapter focuses on DDL declaration mechanics: syntax, naming, ON DELETE/ON UPDATE actions, and validation against existing data
This chapter only discusses foreign keys in the context of normalization
There is no difference; the two chapters cover identical material
original_questions.explanation: The conceptual role of foreign keys (referential integrity) was covered earlier; this chapter's angle is purely the SQL syntax and validation mechanics used to declare and manage them.
